tip: 'La prego di' is a highly formal request formula used when addressing someone as 'Lei'.
'In riferimento a' is a standard opening for formal letters; here 'a' and 'la' merge into 'alla'.
'Vale la pena sottolineare' is literally 'it's worth the pain to underline', a standard formula for adding emphasis.
'Con la presente' is a highly formal opening for official communications.
Pair 'quanto più' with 'tanto meno' for 'the more... the less': 'Quanto più ci penso, tanto meno capisco'.
For a formal command, use the subjunctive, not the 'tu' form: to someone you call 'Lei', 'prendi' becomes 'prenda', as in 'Prenda la prima a sinistra'.
The 'è... che' frame spotlights one element: 'È proprio questo che volevo dire' = THIS is what I wanted to say.
In affirmative commands the pronoun attaches to the end of the verb: 'Ricordami' = 'ricorda' + 'mi' (remind me).
'Per quanto' before an adjective means however or no matter how: 'per quanto controversa' = however controversial.
As a subject, Italian uses the plain infinitive where English uses -ing: 'Imparare una lingua' = learning a language.
A lone past participle up front means after or once something was done: 'Superato l'esame' = once the exam was passed, and the main clause follows.
'Sia che... sia che' means 'whether... or', and both halves take the subjunctive: 'sia che piova sia che splenda'.
Front a quantity with 'di', then resume it with 'ne': 'Di pazienza, ne servirà molta' = of patience, a lot will be needed.
An infinitive can act as a noun, taking 'il', 'suo' and adjectives: 'il suo continuo lamentarsi' = his constant complaining.
An opening past participle agrees with its noun: 'Letta la lettera' uses feminine 'letta' to match 'la lettera'.
Put 'il' in front of an infinitive to make it a noun subject: 'Il vivere in città' = living in the city.
In formal Italian a past participle can stand alone as a whole clause: 'Ciò premesso' = that having been stated.
'Fermo restando' is literally 'remaining firm', a frozen legal opener meaning while something stays in force.
An article before an infinitive turns it into a noun where English uses -ing: 'L'aver studiato' = having studied.
'Per quanto' meaning 'however much' normally takes the subjunctive: 'per quanto la questione possa sembrare irrilevante'.
'A meno che' (unless) takes an extra 'non' that isn't a real negative: 'a meno che non cambino le regole' = unless the rules change.
'Capire'-type verbs add '-isc-' in the present and keep it in the subjunctive: 'capiscano' = (that) they understand.
In the past subjunctive with 'essere', the participle agrees with the subject: 'festa' is feminine, so 'sia stata', not 'stato'.
'Il che' refers back to the whole preceding statement, not a single noun: 'il che è quasi un miracolo' = which is almost a miracle.
'Bisogna' has no subject, so use 'bisogna che' plus the subjunctive: 'Bisogna che io studi' = I need to study.
For an informal negative command, use 'non' plus the infinitive, not the present tense: 'Non bere' means don't drink.
After 'a meno che', the 'non' carries no negative meaning: 'tu non voglia' means unless you want, not unless you don't want.
Italian can form the passive with 'venire' instead of 'essere': 'il contratto venga firmato' means the contract be signed.
Colloquial 'mica' can replace 'non' entirely: 'Mica male' = not bad at all.
'Volerci' means it takes (time). Its past uses 'essere', so 'voluti' agrees with 'giorni', masculine plural.
